newsitem.title: USA: Pork prices soar, grains and coffee tumble.
newsitem.headline: Pork prices soar, grains and coffee tumble.

text.p: Pork prices soared on Thursday after Japan said it was considering cutting a duty on imports of pork due to rising domestic prices.

In other markets, grain and coffee prices fell and oil prices closed mostly steady. The Knight Ridder Commodity Research Bureau index of 17 commodity futures ended 2.46 points lower on the day at 241.62.

At the Chicago Mercantile Exchange, the June hog contract closed up the allowable 2.00-cent a pound daily limit at 82.325 cents and pork bellies for delivery in May closed at 80.175 cents, up 1.875 cents.

Japan, the top U.S. customer for farm goods, initially said it would keep a tariff on pork imports until July 1 despite Taiwan's banning of pork exports on March 20 due to a virulent outbreak of hog foot and mouth disease.

Taiwan had been shipping more than 16,000 metric tons of pork a month to Japan before the ban. The island supplied 40 to 45 percent of Japan's pork imports, compared to U.S. pork's 22 percent market share.

But Masayuki Takahashi, Japan's vice minister of agriculture, said that since pork prices have risen sharply in Japan and could go higher, Japan was considering cutting the tariff it slapped on pork imports in July 1996.
"If domestic pork prices keep rising and damage local consumers' interests, we may have to cut import tariff rates," Takahashi told Reuters in Tokyo on Thursday.

Prospects for higher pork exports to Japan, South Korea and other customers who had relied on Taiwan have boosted U.S. prices sharply since the news. It has also boosted the prospects of meat exporters.

"We view the hog disease problems in Taiwan, currently the largest exporter of pork to Japan, as a multi-year opportunity," Dain Bosworth brokerage analyst Bonnie Wittenburg said on Thursday in changing its rating to "buy" from "hold" for shares of Virginia-based pork producer Smithfield Foods.
"The disease outbreak...could forever change Taiwan's and America's market share in Japan," Wittenburg said.
At the Chicago Board of Trade, grain and soybean prices fell sharply as weekly export shipments fell below the estimates of most analysts and crop weather improved.
Wheat for May delivery closed down 13-1/2 cents a bushel at $3.75, while May corn closed 7-1/2 cents lower at $3.01 and May soybeans ended 12-1/2 cents lower at $8.71.

The Agriculture Department on Thursday said soybean export sales in the week ended March 27 totaled 216,400 metric tons, below expectations for 300,000 to 400,000 tons and 44 percent below last week. Soybeans hit new 8-1/2-year highs earlier this week on booming exports, tight stocks and heavy processor demand.

"Today was a reaction to disappointing export sales," said Mario Balletto, oilseeds analyst with Merrill Lynch. "That set the tone. I think we have priced buyers out of the market. The question is, have we priced them out enough?"
Corn exports of 323,100 tons were also below expectations for 450,000 to 600,000 tons.

At the Coffee Sugar and Cocoa Exchange in New York, coffee futures closed sharply lower as commodity funds sold off, traders said. Coffee for delivery in May closed 15.45 cents a pound lower at 177.70 cents.
Traders said rising coffee stocks in the United States had taken some of the heat out of the speculative fever that doubled coffee prices between December and March.
In February, coffee stocks rose 204,000 132-pound bags to 1,546,000 bags, according to the Green Coffee Association of New York. Figures for March stocks are due on April 15.
At the New York Mercantile Exchange, oil prices ended on a firm note as traders went bargain hunting following a sell-off Wednesday amid increasing crude oil imports and supplies.
Gasoline for May delivery ended 0.29 cent higher at 60.90 cents a gallon and May heating oil closed up 0.74 cent a gallon at 53.26 cents. May delivery crude oil closed unchanged at $19.47 a barrel.
"We had been oversold after the market weakened on high imports. By the end of April, we could see better gasoline demand," said Mike De Luca, trader with Prudential Securities.

The American Petroleum Institute said on Tuesday that U.S. crude oil imports rose sharply to 7.7 million barrels a day in the week ended on March 28 from 6.8 million a week earlier due to an influx of West African crude oil.
